transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration (calendar): 62 mins
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (Redwood Infra), Carlos Mendez (HelixAI ML Eng), Priya Rao (HelixAI Platform), Evan Li (HelixAI CTO)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on per-model tuning for inference performance: Llama/Mistral/Qwen differences, MoE routing overheads, RoPE scaling behavior, KV cache patterns, batching/throughput tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints for benchmarking. Agreed next steps: share benchmark artifacts, run targeted bench of Llama-70B with KV cache, and propose dedicated capacity sizing for HelixAI POC.

Topics:
- Latency vs throughput tradeoffs and batching windows
- Continuous KV cache behavior for long context (10k+ tokens)
- Quantization impact on model quality and throughput (4-bit vs 8-bit mixed)
- MoE routing costs and when MoE is the right fit
- RoPE scaling and position interpolation issues across model families
- VPC/on-prem benchmarking constraints and telemetry needs

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, quick intros and then get into the deep bits -- Samira you'll lead the perf stuff?
[00:18] Samira Khan: yup, hi all, SE at Redwood, I focus on runtime and perf, a few slides but mostly logs and numbers, and we'll swap through examples with Llama, Mistral and Qwen
[00:35] Carlos Mendez: thanks, Carlos here, I run model infra at HelixAI, main constraint is long context chat -- our prompts average 6k tokens, some long docs hit ~12k, and we need p95 latency under 800ms for user interactions
[00:50] Priya Rao: Priya here, platform lead, concerned about network egress and VPC peering costs if we do hosted, also KMS for keys
[01:05] Evan Li: Evan, CTO -- want to understand MoE routing overhead and whether it's worth the cost for summarization pipelines
[01:20] Samira Khan: ok quick agenda slide (link: slides.redwood/deepdive), then go to bench results, then Q/A and next steps
[01:36] Samira Khan: first, high level, Llama family generally has stable RoPE implementations, Mistral tends to be cheaper per-token for the same quality at short contexts, Qwen is somewhere in between but has differences on attention kernel shapes which affect batching and memory layout
[01:55] Jordan Park: (overlap) and we saw -- just to flag -- customers who need 8k+ contexts often prefer pinning to dedicated capacity because of KV cache hit ratios, so cost predictability is a thing
[02:12] Samira Khan: right, to unpack KV cache: continuous requests that share prefixes can use KV cache to avoid recomputing past key/value blocks. In practice we see 30-60% token compute savings for sessioned chat, but that depends on prompt overlap and how you shard tokens across requests
[02:36] Carlos Mendez: quick q: is KV cache hot-sharded across GPUs or per replica? we plan multi-GPU serving in case one shard fails
[02:52] Alex Morgan: KV cache is sharded per-GPU when model sharding (tensor-parallel) is used; for data parallel replicas each replica keeps its own cache. We've got options for remote KV cache in upcoming release but it's higher latency right now
[03:10] Priya Rao: so remote KV cache increases network egress, right? that could blow our egress budget
[03:22] Samira Khan: yes, remote cache has network overhead; we recommend co-locating cache or using dedicated instances to keep cross-host calls low
[03:36] Samira Khan: moving to batching: we typically use dynamic batching with a latency SLO cap -- increasing batch window raises throughput but at p95 latency cost. Example: for Llama-70B we saw throughput double when increasing batching window from 10ms to 40ms but p95 jumped from 420ms to 720ms
[04:00] Evan Li: and is that window configurable per route? we have mixed-criticality routes
[04:12] Jordan Park: yes per-route configs -- you can set max wait, allow burst capacity, and route critical traffic to low-latency pool 
[04:24] Samira Khan: quantization: we did 4-bit q4_K_mixed on Mistral and saw ~1.8x throughput vs float16 with low degradation on our eval set, but on Qwen the same quant profile had slightly worse quality -- likely due to its layernorm/activation ordering
[04:50] Carlos Mendez: hmm we care about rouge/accuracy for summarization -- how do you validate quality regressions?
[05:04] Samira Khan: we run paired evals on customer prompts + Redwood eval harness, threshold alerts if generation drift exceeds configurable delta; we can also do partial-quant rollouts per-model version for canary checks
[05:20] Priya Rao: can you explain MoE routing cost -- I read MoE can be compute efficient but routing is expensive?
[05:36] Samira Khan: good question -- MoE gives sparse, larger capacity by only activating a subset of experts per token. That lowers FLOPs for inference per token in theory, but the routing/gating introduces scatter/gather and extra all-to-all patterns across devices for expert-parallel shards. If your requests are short or you have high concurrency, routing overhead and increased memory movement can negate the FLOP savings
[06:04] Alex Morgan: also important: in multi-GPU setups, MoE often requires more interconnect bandwidth. For on-prem customers with limited NVLink/IB, routing stalls can increase latency variance
[06:20] Evan Li: so for our summarization pipelines which are medium-length (~1k tokens) and heavy concurrency, MoE might not help?
[06:32] Samira Khan: likely not -- MoE is most attractive when you need very large capacity for occasional heavy tokens or low concurrency workloads where expert sparsity can be exploited. For steady high concurrency, mixture-of-experts often increases tail latency unless you have a custom infra optimized for the routing pattern
[06:55] Jordan Park: (interruption) also licensing/cost -- MoE models sometimes have different tooling and provisioning requirements which can complicate Dedicated pricing
[07:08] Carlos Mendez: got it. RoPE scaling -- we've seen weird position shifts when we extend contexts beyond the model pretrain max, e.g., 2x position leading to repetition. Any guidance?
[07:24] Samira Khan: RoPE scaling is tricky: some model families use absolute sin/cos, others use rotary embeddings with frequency scaling. For Llama and Qwen, linear RoPE extrapolation usually works ok up to ~1.5x pretrain length, beyond that you see attenuation in position salience. We sometimes apply linear interpolation or rope-fixups in tokenization to mitigate but it's model-specific
[07:48] Priya Rao: is that something Redwood automates?
[07:55] Samira Khan: we have RoPE scaling heuristics in our model runner; for customer POCs we can test multiple scaling strategies and report quality tradeoffs
[08:10] Jordan Park: let's walk through a concrete bench: Samira, you shared a Llama-70B baseline earlier?
[08:18] Samira Khan: yes quick numbers (link: benchmark.redwood/helixai-llama-70b): baseline float16 single node, 8x A100-80GB, 2k token generation, unbatched p50 220ms per token, p95 480ms; with dynamic batching (max wait 30ms) throughput improved 1.9x, p95 rose to 640ms. With q4_mixed quant on the same node we saw overall token/sec +1.7x and p95 about 560ms -- quality delta small on our prompted evals
[08:52] Carlos Mendez: those p95s are borderline for us, we need under 800ms -- so seems ok, but sessioned 10k context will change that, right?
[09:03] Samira Khan: yes; with KV cache warm and high prefix reuse our end-to-end latency per new token drops significantly because we don't re-encode the whole prefix. For 10k context with 80% prefix overlap we measured effective compute reduction of ~45% on token generation
[09:20] Priya Rao: what's the memory footprint of keeping a 10k token KV cache for Llama-70B?
[09:32] Alex Morgan: very roughly a 70B model with 16-bit KV entries is large -- per token KV overhead depends on head dims; practical numbers we saw were ~1.2-1.8GB per 1k tokens per replica for certain model layouts; so 10k could be ~12-18GB just for KV structures, so plan GPU memory accordingly or use offload strategies
[09:59] Carlos Mendez: oh that high -- we need to account for that in Dedicated sizing then
[10:10] Samira Khan: yes, and options: 1) shard KV across GPUs; 2) use quantized KV (reduce precision) for storage; 3) evict older prefix entries if not frequently used
[10:28] Evan Li: about quantized KV -- does that harm generation quality?
[10:36] Samira Khan: light quant on KV (8-bit) tends to be fine; aggressive 4-bit on KV can have small impact but depends on model sensitivity. We recommend targetted A/B tests on your prompts
[10:50] Priya Rao: network and VPC concerns -- we want to do a POC on-prem in our colo, can Redwood run a private deployment?
[11:02] Jordan Park: yes Redwood Private, you can run control plane in our managed mode or self-host the control plane; for colo we often do a hybrid: control plane out and data plane in-customer VPC, KMS integrated. We'll share the SOW options
[11:18] Priya Rao: what's the telemetry footprint for private deployments? we have strict audit windows
[11:28] Alex Morgan: telemetry can be configured -- we can redact tokens, only ship anonymized metrics and traces; audit logging is supported with configurable retention to meet SOC2/ISO requirements
[11:42] Samira Khan: back to kernels and batch shapes: Qwen models had non-uniform attention head sizes which made fused kernels less efficient than Llama in some cases. That meant our batching scheduler had to prefer batch sizes that matched memory alignment, otherwise we saw fragmentation on CUDA memory and lower utilization
[12:10] Carlos Mendez: interesting -- so does Redwood expose kernel-level telemetry so our infra team can tune GPU packing?
[12:20] Alex Morgan: yes we expose per-kernel timelines, utilization heatmaps, and memory fragmentation stats in the Console; we can share guidance templates for packing strategies by model family
[12:33] Jordan Park: if we talk pricing, dedicated sizing for this workload (10k contexts, 3k qps peak concurrent sessions ~200) would usually be a cluster of n1 nodes -- I'll follow up with a concrete sizing doc. (link: examples.redwood/dedicated-sizing)
[12:50] Priya Rao: regarding security, we need SAML SSO and RBAC for our team -- supported?
[12:58] Jordan Park: yes SAML, SCIM, fine-grained RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Redwood Private and Dedicated customers
[13:10] Evan Li: any customer stories with MoE where it actually improved latencies?
[13:18] Samira Khan: we had one media customer where MoE worked because they had very low concurrency but needed huge capacity for niche topics -- in that case the sparse activation reduced cost. But it's the exception, not the rule
[13:32] Carlos Mendez: ok makes sense. about RoPE again -- we sometimes have models that were fine at 2k pretrain but we push to 8k -- will Redwood help produce fine-tuned ropemaps?
[13:46] Samira Khan: we can run rope-scaling experiments: linear extrapolation, frequency rescaling, and windowed attention emulation. We'll produce a small eval matrix showing perplexity and generation quality versus context length
[14:04] Priya Rao: any recommendations for parallelism strategy? TP/DP/MoE mixing -- our cluster is 8x80GB GPUs with NVLink
[14:18] Alex Morgan: with 8x80GB, prefer tensor-parallel with data parallel replicas for throughput; MoE complicates shard placement. If KV cache large, consider model parallel strategies that keep KV local to a subset of GPUs to avoid cross-host traffic
[14:38] Jordan Park: can we quickly call out risk areas for the POC?
[14:44] Samira Khan: yes: 1) KV memory footprint overruns; 2) MoE routing stalls if attempted; 3) quantization quality regression on Qwen; 4) network egress for remote KV or remote telemetry. We'll add mitigation strategies in the follow-up doc
[15:00] Carlos Mendez: thanks, that's helpful, for the bench we'll need the exec summary and raw logs to justify infra spend
[15:10] Jordan Park: Samira will share the benchmark sheet and raw logs; Jordan will share cost ranges and security docs; Carlos/Priya will provide prompt set and short-lived VPC access
[15:25] (brief pause)
[15:40] Samira Khan: quick demo of kernel timeline (screen share noted): see here the attention kernel on Qwen spikes with odd memory stride causing 20% lower occupancy
[15:58] Carlos Mendez: hmm can you capture the kernel args? we can try re-tuning our CUDA mem allocator on-prem
[16:08] Samira Khan: yes we'll attach per-kernel arg dumps in the bench zip. note some of the variable names in our trace are auto-annotated and sometimes wrong -- please ignore typos like qwen->qwenx in traces
[16:24] Priya Rao: regarding egress again, if we host in a cloud region to save dev time, can we pin region to reduce inter-region egress?
[16:34] Jordan Park: yes region pinning and routing policies are supported; also policy-level fallbacks to local models when cross-region latency too high
[16:44] Evan Li: on the topic of batching windows, can Redwood do micro-batching with low jitter guarantees?
[16:54] Samira Khan: we have continuous batching with jitter smoothing; you can set max latency and probability thresholds for jitter allowed. For strict low-jitter usecases we recommend a dedicated low-latency pool with small batch windows and extra reserved capacity
[17:12] Carlos Mendez: what about caching strategies for multi-tenant -- we want tenant isolation but also reuse across tenants for common system prompts
[17:26] Alex Morgan: we support namespaced KV cache and shared read-only caches for common prompts; isolation and ACLs are enforced. You can also pin certain caches to a tenant-specific pool to avoid noisy neighbors
[17:40] Samira Khan: other gotcha -- when you quantize weights, some libraries move compute from GEMM to custom kernels; that can change the optimal batch size, so expect to re-run kernel packing tests after quantization
[17:58] Priya Rao: good note. ok last quick: for evaluation thresholds, how do you signal quality regressions?
[18:08] Samira Khan: Redwood Optimize runs automated eval suites against baseline metrics and can alert via Slack/email when deltas exceed configured thresholds; we also do human-in-the-loop review on critical deploys
[18:20] Jordan Park: wrap time -- recap of action items and next steps (see metadata). We'll aim to have bench draft by 2026-05-19 and a follow-up sync the week after. Thanks everyone
[18:36] Carlos Mendez: thanks, appreciate the thoroughness
[18:44] Evan Li: thanks all
[18:50] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms and some auto-annotation errors. Shared artifacts: slides.redwood/deepdive, benchmark.redwood/helixai-llama-70b, examples.redwood/dedicated-sizing, security.redwood/soc2-summary (links provided by Jordan).
